sections.heading: Manager Lionel Danford appeals for funds to save deaf sevens campaign
sections.body: The Fiji men’s and women’s deaf rugby sevens teams are facing a major financial hurdle ahead of the upcoming World Deaf Rugby Sevens Championship in Tokyo. Team manager Lionel Danford revealed a funding gap of up to $70,000 remains for daily expenses and camp preparations, despite valuable kit sponsorship from PacificAus Sports. Despite these hardships, preparations continue, including a crucial scrimmage session scheduled against Osea Kolinisau’s national sevens side.

sections.heading: Eddie O’Sullivan warns Andy Farrell after Leinster’s international front-row scrum struggles
sections.body: Former head coach Eddie O’Sullivan has flagged South Africa’s "frightening" scrum dominance as a major concern for Andy Farrell ahead of the autumn internationals. Following Leinster’s recent 26-20 defeat to the Sharks, where a Test-strength front-row including Andrew Porter and Ronan Kelleher conceded eight scrum penalties, O’Sullivan suggested the Springboks’ physical power is becoming a problem for World Rugby. While acknowledging the challenge is not unique to Ireland, he noted that South Africa "take you to the woodshed" through sheer physical attrition.

sections.body: Eddie O'Sullivan says the Springboks have become 'almost unbeatable' at scrum time, a worry for Andy Farrell before Ireland host them again this autumn. The former Ireland coach's comments follow a bruising week for Leinster's Test front-row of Andrew Porter, Ronan Kelleher and Thomas Clarkson, beaten up at scrum time by the Sharks in Durban — eight scrum penalties conceded and Clarkson sin-binned. It echoes last year's Aviva Test, when Porter and Paddy McCarthy were both yellow-carded for scrum infringements against South Africa.

lead.why: Freshest, highest-scoring story and the only genuine men's Ireland angle — a direct read on Farrell's autumn scrum worries.

sections.heading: Scottish Rugby faces continued legal uncertainty over stalled concussion lawsuit
sections.body: The legal challenge regarding brain injuries in rugby union remains in a state of uncertainty as claimants navigate a multi-million-pound financial hurdle. Although former players won a significant court battle in August to prevent World Rugby and Scottish Rugby from having the case thrown out, the litigation is currently hindered by a £2.8 million bill for legal costs. This impasse must be resolved before the group, which includes several former internationals, can proceed with their pursuit of damages for neurological conditions.

sections.heading: Scottish Rugby concussion case remains stalled over unpaid legal fees
sections.body: The group lawsuit brought by ex-players against World Rugby, the WRU, the RFU and Scottish Rugby remains unresolved. Claimants won a court battle in August, when judges refused to throw the case out, but the action stalled again this week: the Guardian reported earlier this week that hundreds of claimants face a £2.8m legal bill, with no resolution reported since. The case stays open only if that fee is settled — for now, there's no word on when, or whether, it will be.

sections.heading: Welsh Rugby Union publishes report justifying the 2028 West Wales professional cull
sections.body: The Welsh Rugby Union has released the 68-page Keystone report detailing the evidence used to decide that only one professional team will represent West Wales from 2028. With Cardiff and the Dragons already granted capital and east licences, the Ospreys and Scarlets must now compete for the remaining slot. Union bosses maintain that funding cannot support four professional sides beyond the 2027-28 season. A final decision on which of the two historic west-Wales clubs will be culled is expected in June 2027.

lead.why: The release of the Keystone report provides the official institutional evidence and data justification for the upcoming reduction of Wales' professional regions.

sections.heading: Les Kiss replaces suspended Hunter Paisami with Isaac Henry for Auckland Test
sections.body: Les Kiss has drafted Isaac Henry into the midfield for Saturday’s Bledisloe Cup opener at Eden Park, replacing the suspended Hunter Paisami. It is the sole change to the starting XV as the Wallabies attempt to end a 40-year winless run at the venue. Kiss described the Auckland ground as a "bloody cool stadium to play at" but warned it can suffocate teams who are not ready. Captain Harry Wilson says the squad is drawing confidence from last year's victory at Ellis Park.

sections.heading: Australia look to break 23-year Eden Park hoodoo against All Blacks
sections.body: The Wallabies face the daunting task of ending a winless run at Eden Park that stretches back to 1986. While the venue remains a fortress where the All Blacks are unbeaten since 1994, coach Les Kiss has maintained consistency, making only one change to his starting side as Isaac Henry replaces the suspended Hunter Paisami. Reflecting on the challenge, Kiss noted: “It’s got its own sense of atmosphere, that really can envelope you and it can suffocate you if you’re not ready.”

lead.why: It is the primary narrative in the rugby press today regarding Australia's immediate objective at Eden Park.

sections.heading: Les Kiss eyes end to 40-year Eden Park Bledisloe Cup drought
sections.body: The All Blacks are Les Kiss's sternest test yet — Australia haven't beaten them at Eden Park since 1986, and the hosts are unbeaten there in 53 Tests stretching back to 1994. Kiss, chasing a breakthrough in Saturday's Bledisloe Cup opener, admits the ground "can suffocate you if you're not ready." New Zealand arrive with selection headaches of their own: fly-half Richie Mo'unga is out with a calf complaint, Ruben Love's season is over after ankle surgery, Damian McKenzie moves to No. 10, and Beauden Barrett returns at full-back.

lead.why: Highest-scored story with genuine new team news — the All Blacks' injury-forced reshuffle — layered onto the Eden Park drought angle, distinct from yesterday's Suaalii wing story.

sections.heading: Japan Sakura 7s Reclaim Gold Medal At The 20th Asian Games
sections.body: The Japan Sakura 7s secured a dramatic 10-5 victory over defending champions China in Aichi to reclaim the gold medal at the 20th Asian Games. In a closely contested final, Japan demonstrated their resilience to return to the top of the podium, a feat last achieved two Games ago. The result provided a boost for Japanese rugby, concluding a weekend where the men’s side also finished on the podium by defeating Korea 17-5 to claim the bronze medal.

lead.why: The Sakura 7s' gold medal win at the Asian Games represents the most significant recent competitive achievement for Japanese rugby.

sections.heading: Japan Rugby Football Union hosts online forum to discuss future values
sections.body: The Japan Rugby Football Union held an online forum this week to mark its centenary, shifting focus toward the long-term societal impact of the game. Rather than focusing on match results, the event explored how the sport’s core values—the spirit of 'No Side', respect for diversity, and 'One Team'—can be integrated into wider social development. Top executives and stakeholders reviewed the union's history while discussing the evolving role of rugby within the modern era.

lead.why: This is a fresh report on the JRFU centenary forum discussing the future of Japanese rugby values.

sections.heading: Japan Rugby League One retreats on naturalised Brave Blossoms eligibility
sections.body: Japan Rugby League One has backtracked on contentious new registration rules that would have classified naturalised, Japanese-passport-holding players as foreigners, limiting their game time and, by extension, their visibility for Brave Blossoms selection. Following legal challenges and a fierce backlash — including a Japan Fair Trade Commission complaint from 27 players — the league confirmed naturalised players who held or had applied for citizenship by May 2025 will be treated as Japanese-born when the new system starts in the 2026-27 season. "The criticism was much stronger than we expected," a league executive admitted.

lead.why: The only story not already covered this week, and editor notes prioritise institutional/regulatory shifts over repeat match reports on the Ireland tour or Asian Games sevens.

sections.heading: Eben Etzebeth and Ox Nché named to start for Sharks derby
sections.body: The Sharks have elevated Springboks duo Eben Etzebeth and Ox Nché to their starting XV for today’s United Rugby Championship clash against the Stormers in Cape Town. Head coach JP Pietersen has overhauled his pack, moving Etzebeth into the second row and Nché to loosehead prop, while captain Andre Esterhuizen retains his place in the midfield. Both sides have opted for a 6-2 bench split, with the Sharks naming Stephan Lewies among the replacements for his second club debut.

sections.heading: Aoife Wafer ruled out of Ireland's WXV tests against South Africa
sections.body: Ireland forward Aoife Wafer will not travel to South Africa for the upcoming WXV Global Series matches. The player has been ruled out of the fixtures scheduled for 24 and 31 October in Cape Town due to an injury sustained during training. Ireland head coach Scott Bemand has named a 30-player squad for the trip, which includes the return of Ruth Campbell following an ankle recovery, while Sam Monaghan remains unavailable for selection due to an Achilles injury.

sections.heading: Steve Lancaster says Springboks 'pretty bullish' on URC, not Super Rugby return
sections.body: NZ Rugby chief executive Steve Lancaster has given the clearest read yet on the Springboks' stance on a possible Super Rugby return, insisting there's no appetite in Pretoria for a switch back. Lancaster says the two unions remain close after Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, but South Africa are committed to the United Rugby Championship for now. 'South Africa are pretty bullish about how things have played out for them,' he said, pointing to the Springboks, URC, Currie Cup and growing participation numbers as evidence it's working.

lead.why: Institutional Super Rugby return talk carries more weight and direct Bok relevance than the women's WXV story or the low-scoring Bledisloe quote, matching the desk's steer toward structural news.
